replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" in "I went to the bank" is represented as the **same token** whether you mean a riverbank or a financial institution.

The AI has no dictionary to look up which one you mean — it has to figure it out from context. That's actually the whole puzzle this lesson is about.

So let's start at the very beginning of what happens the moment you hit send.

---

The first thing an LLM does is break your text into **tokens** — small chunks that are usually a word or part of a word.

"Tokenization" isn't splitting on spaces. The word "unhappiness" might become three tokens: "un", "happi", "ness". Each token gets converted into a number, because math is all the model actually does.

---

GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these tokens — so every prompt you write becomes a sequence of numbers drawn from that list.

Think of it like sheet music: your words become a score the model can compute with.

---

[CHECK]Before the model does anything else with those numbers — before it predicts a single word — what do you think it needs to figure out about each token?[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and that detail about word boundaries matters more than it seems (it's why "strawberry" can trip models up when counting letters).

Now here's what those numbers actually *do* next.

---

Each token gets placed in an **embedding space** — imagine a vast map where tokens that tend to appear in similar contexts end up near each other.

"King" and "queen" land close together. "Bank" (money) and "interest rate" cluster in one region; "bank" (river) and "current" cluster in another.

---

But a token's position on that map shifts depending on its neighbors — and that's the **attention mechanism** at work.

When the model reads "I went to the bank to deposit my check," attention lets "bank" borrow meaning from "deposit" and "check," pulling it toward the financial cluster. Swap in "I sat by the bank and watched the river," and the same token drifts toward the water cluster.

---

Every token essentially asks every other token: *how relevant are you to figuring out what I mean?* The answers get weighted and combined — thousands of times, in parallel, across many layers.

That's how context sorts out ambiguity, without any lookup table or dictionary.

---

[CHECK]In the sentence "She plays the bass in a jazz band," which other word do you think the attention mechanism would weight most heavily to figure out what "bass" means — and why?[/CHECK]

replies.user: The embeddings put similar meanings near each other, so the model can use context — like 'bank' ending up near money words or river words depending on the sentence. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter for the current one.
replies.raw:
You've got the core idea — attention is essentially a relevance-weighting system, and you named it precisely.

(I'll hold the "bass" question since you moved on — we can come back if anything feels fuzzy.)

Now for the final piece: what the model actually *produces*.

---

After attention has done its work, the model doesn't "choose" a word the way you'd pick from a menu. It assigns a **probability** to every token in its 100,000-token vocabulary.

"The cat sat on the ___" — "mat", "floor", "couch" all score high. "Tuesday" scores near zero.

---

The model then samples from those probabilities and outputs one token. Then it does the whole thing again — feeding that new token back in, running attention, generating the next probability distribution — one token at a time, in a loop.

This is **next-token prediction**: the entire output of an LLM is just this process repeating until it hits a stopping point.

---

Here's the key implication: the model is optimizing for *what token is plausible given everything before it* — not for what's true, not for what's useful, just for what fits the pattern.

That single fact explains a lot about both what LLMs are good at and where they go wrong.

---

Now let's put this to work.

**Your exercise:**

Here's a sentence with two blanks:

*"The surgeon scrubbed her hands before entering the ___, then later explained the ___ to the anxious family."*

1. For the first blank: would an LLM predict the next token with **high confidence** or **low confidence**? Name the most likely token and explain why in terms of tokenization, embedding, and attention.

2. For the second blank: same question — high or low confidence? Name the most likely token and explain why.

replies.user: It predicts the next token by probability — so 'The cat sat on the' makes 'mat' very likely. It's not looking up an answer, it's continuing a learned pattern.
replies.raw:
That's a clean summary of next-token prediction — you've got it.

But I need your attempt at the actual exercise before we can wrap up. It's where the real test of understanding happens.

Here's the sentence again:

*"The surgeon scrubbed her hands before entering the ___, then later explained the ___ to the anxious family."*

**1.** First blank — high or low confidence? What's the most likely token, and why (use what you know about attention and embeddings)?

**2.** Second blank — high or low confidence? What's the most likely token, and why?

Take a shot at both — even a rough answer tells me a lot.

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — in your sentence, the slot right after the last two words, where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot like right after the opening word, where several continuations ('a', 'the', a noun) are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.
replies.raw:

But I need you to apply it to *these specific blanks*, not the principle in the abstract. The exercise only works if you name the tokens and explain the attention story for each one.

Just two tokens, two confidence calls, two quick reasons. Give it a go.

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" — as in a riverbank — and "bank" as in a place to deposit money are, at first, **the exact same token** to an LLM.

The model doesn't know which meaning you intend until it does something more sophisticated. More on that in a moment.

---

First, let's talk about what a token actually is.

When you type a prompt, the model doesn't read letters or words the way you do. It breaks your text into chunks called **tokens** — roughly syllable-sized pieces.

[EX]"Unbelievable" might become three tokens: "Un", "believ", "able". A short common word like "cat" is usually one token. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these chunks.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokens are the basic unit of language an LLM works with — not letters, not full words, but chunks that get converted into numbers.[/KEY]

Every token gets turned into a number, and that number points to a location in a giant mathematical space. Words with similar meanings end up near each other in that space — that's called an **embedding**.

---

Before we go further:

[Q]
What does an LLM actually receive when you type a prompt?
A) The words exactly as you typed them, stored as text
B) A sequence of numbered chunks (tokens) representing your text
C) A recording of your keystrokes sent to a search engine
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A sequence of numbered chunks (tokens) representing your text
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the model never sees raw text, only those numbered chunks.

Now here's where it gets interesting: a sequence of numbers alone doesn't tell you much about *meaning*. That's where the **attention mechanism** comes in.

When the model processes your tokens, it doesn't treat each one in isolation. It looks at every other token in your prompt and asks, in effect: *which of these other tokens should I pay attention to right now?*

[EX]In the sentence "I went to the bank to fish," the token "bank" gets pulled toward "fish" and "went" — and away from anything money-related. That's attention sorting out the riverbank meaning, not the financial one.[/EX]

[KEY]Attention lets each token "look at" the surrounding tokens to figure out its meaning in context — it's how the model resolves ambiguity.[/KEY]

This happens across many layers, with the model building a richer and richer picture of what your prompt means.

And once it has that picture? It uses everything it learned during training to do one deceptively simple thing: predict the single most likely *next* token. Then it does it again.

And again. That's the whole output — one token at a time.

---

[Q]
Why can an LLM figure out that "bank" means riverbank in "I went to the bank to fish"?
A) It looks up "bank" in a dictionary and picks the most common definition
B) It checks which meaning appears more often in its training data overall
C) It weighs how strongly nearby tokens like "fish" pull the meaning in one direction
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) It looks up "bank" in a dictionary and picks the most common definition
replies.raw:
That's a tempting idea — but it's actually the opposite of how this works.

A dictionary lookup treats every word in isolation. The model would always pick the same definition of "bank," no matter what surrounded it.

Attention is specifically about *relationships between tokens in your sentence*. The token "fish" doesn't just sit there — it actively pulls "bank" toward the riverbank meaning, because during training the model saw those words near each other in that context thousands of times.

There's no dictionary. There's no lookup. Just tokens influencing each other.

---

Try it this way: imagine "bank" in two sentences.

*"I went to the bank to deposit a check."*
*"I went to the bank to fish."*

The word "bank" is identical in both. What's different is everything *around* it — and attention is the mechanism that notices that difference.

[Q]
What does the attention mechanism actually do?
A) It searches a database for the correct word definition
B) It lets each token be shaped by the other tokens surrounding it
C) It picks the most frequent meaning from the training data, regardless of context
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) It lets each token be shaped by the other tokens surrounding it
replies.raw:
You nailed it — and now you have the full picture of what happens inside an LLM when you type a prompt.

Tokens go in → attention figures out meaning from context → the model predicts the next token → repeat.

---

**Here's your exercise:**

Look at this sentence:

*"After the surgery, the doctor handed the nurse the ___."*

**Part 3:** Now think of a sentence where the blank would be genuinely LOW confidence for almost any word — where many different completions seem equally plausible. Write that sentence and explain why the model would be uncertain.

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is the **same token** whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings account.

The AI doesn't know which one you mean — at least not yet.

That's the puzzle tokenization creates, and it's the first thing that happens the moment you hit send.

---

When you type a prompt, the text doesn't go in as words. It gets chopped into **tokens** — chunks that are sometimes a whole word, sometimes just part of one (like "un-" or "-ing"), sometimes punctuation.

Each token gets converted to a number, because math is all a neural network can actually do.

GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 of these tokens.

---

So "I went to the bank" becomes something like: [40, 1816, 284, 262, 3331] — a list of numbers, not a sentence.

The model has no idea what "bank" means yet. That's the job of the next layer.

---

[CHECK]Before I explain how the model figures out which "bank" you meant — what do you think it would need to look at?[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and that detail about sub-word splits matters more than it sounds, because it means even a single word can carry multiple tokens with different meanings depending on context.

Now, here's how the model figures out which "bank" you meant.

---

The mechanism is called **attention**, and it's the core innovation that made modern LLMs possible.

Instead of reading tokens one by one in order, attention lets every token "look at" every other token in the prompt simultaneously — and decide which ones are most relevant to its own meaning.

---

So in "I went to the bank to deposit my paycheck," the token for "bank" gets pulled toward "deposit" and "paycheck" — and away from "river" or "water."

That's how the same token resolves to the right meaning: context votes on it.

---

The original paper that introduced this mechanism is worth knowing by name.

[SOURCE: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need" (2017, the original Transformer paper) — arxiv.org]

---

[CHECK]Here's a quick test: in the sentence "She sat by the bank and watched the current," which other tokens would attention pull "bank" toward — and which would it pull "current" toward?[/CHECK]

replies.user: The embeddings put similar meanings near each other, so the model can use context — like 'bank' ending up near money words or river words depending on the sentence. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter for the current one.
replies.raw:
Good instinct on context shaping meaning — though I want to flag one small thing: attention doesn't just look *backward* at earlier tokens. It looks at *all* tokens in the prompt at once, in both directions simultaneously.

Also, I'll hold the embedding space idea for a moment — let's land the last piece first, because it's the one that ties everything together.

---

Once attention has figured out what each token *means* in context, the model does something surprisingly simple: it **predicts the next token**.

Not the next word. The next token — the single most probable continuation, drawn from that vocabulary of ~100,000 options.

Then it appends that token and predicts the next one. And the next. That's the entire generation loop.

---

Think about this sentence: "The cat sat on the ___"

The model assigns a probability to every token in its vocabulary. "Mat" scores very high. "Roof" scores lower but plausible.

"Democracy" scores near zero.

The model picks from that distribution — which is why you sometimes get surprising but grammatical outputs.

---

This also explains hallucination, by the way: the model is optimizing for *plausible continuations*, not *true ones*. But that's the next lesson.

---

[CHECK]If I gave the model "The sky is ___," which kind of completion would get high confidence — and why does that tell you something about what the model is actually doing?[/CHECK]

replies.user: It predicts the next token by probability — so 'The cat sat on the' makes 'mat' very likely. It's not looking up an answer, it's continuing a learned pattern.
replies.raw:
You nailed the key point — it's pattern continuation, not lookup. That distinction is what most people get wrong about AI.

Now let's put this to work.

---

The model has no dictionary to look up which meaning is right. It has to figure that out from context alone.

When you type a prompt, the very first thing an LLM does is break your text into **tokens** — chunks that are roughly (but not exactly) words. "Unhappy" might be one token; "unbelievable" might be split into two. Each token gets converted into a number, because the model is, at its core, a math machine.

Exactly right — math operations need numbers as input, and tokens give the model a clean numerical handle on language.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those numbers aren't just IDs on a list — they get placed in a high-dimensional **embedding space**, where meaning becomes geometry. Words used in similar contexts end up close together.

"King" and "queen" cluster near each other; "bank" (money) clusters near "loan" and "interest," while "bank" (river) clusters near "shore" and "current."

This is how the model starts to sort out that ambiguity.

Then comes the **attention mechanism** — the model looks at every other token in your prompt and asks, for each one: *how relevant is this token to understanding the current one?* For "bank" in "I went to the bank to deposit my check," the word "deposit" gets high attention weight, pulling "bank" toward the financial cluster.

Think of it as the model taking a vote across your whole sentence before it decides what anything means.

replies.raw:
You've got the core idea — attention is the mechanism that makes context actually *do* something, pulling meaning in the right direction.

Now for the payoff: what does all that work *produce*?

After tokenization, embedding, and attention, the model does one thing: it predicts the **next token**. That's it. It looks at everything before the cursor and outputs a probability distribution — a ranked list of what token is most likely to come next.

"The cat sat on the ___" produces very high probability for "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability for "democracy" or "seventeen."

The model picks from that distribution, appends the token, then *repeats the whole process* — now predicting the token after that one. Your entire response is built one token at a time, each prediction feeding the next.

This means fluency is baked in from the start. The model is optimized to produce *plausible continuations* — which is powerful, but also why it can sound confident even when it's wrong. More on that in a later lesson.

Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" in "I went to the bank" is the **same token** whether you mean a riverbank or a place to deposit money.

The AI doesn't know which one you mean just from the word itself — and yet it almost always gets it right. How?

That's exactly what this lesson is about.

---

Let's start at the very beginning: **tokenization**.

When you type a prompt, the model doesn't read words the way you do. It first chops your text into chunks called *tokens* — sometimes a whole word, sometimes just part of one.

[KEY]A token is the basic unit an LLM reads: roughly a word or word-fragment, converted into a number.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer works from a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. The word "unhappiness" might split into "un", "happiness" — two tokens, two numbers.[/EX]

Every token becomes a number, and that number points to a location in a giant mathematical space. Words with similar meanings end up near each other in that space — that's called an *embedding*.

---

Before we go further — quick check:

[Q]
When an LLM reads your prompt, what does it actually process?
A) The letters of each word, one by one
B) Numbers that represent chunks of text called tokens
C) A search-engine index of relevant web pages
ANS: B
[/Q]

Exactly right — the model never sees raw letters or web pages, just those numbers.

Now here's where it gets interesting: having numbers isn't enough. The model still needs to figure out that "bank" means *money* and not *river*. That's where the **attention mechanism** comes in.

Attention lets every token "look at" every other token in your prompt and decide which ones matter most for its meaning.

[KEY]Attention is how the model uses context — "bank" next to "deposit" pulls toward finance; next to "fishing" it pulls toward water.[/KEY]

[EX]In the sentence "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired," attention figures out that "it" refers to "animal" — not "street" — by weighing which earlier token fits best.[/EX]

After attention has sorted out meaning from context, the model does one final thing: it predicts the next token.

It doesn't retrieve a stored answer. It looks at all the tokens so far and asks: *given everything before this, what number comes next?* Then it does that again, and again, until the response is complete.

---

[Q]
Why does next-token prediction sometimes produce confident-sounding wrong answers?
A) The model skips the attention step when it's uncertain
B) It optimizes for what sounds plausible, not for what's true
C) It only predicts tokens it has seen before in training
ANS: B
[/Q]

The model can produce token combinations it has never seen before. What it's really doing is picking whatever continuation *seems most likely* given the context, and "likely" is shaped by training patterns, not limited to copying them exactly.

Option B is the key idea: the model is optimized for **plausibility**, not truth. A fluent, confident-sounding sequence scores well during training even if the underlying claim is wrong.

That's actually one of the most important things to understand about LLMs — and we'll see it cause real problems in a later lesson.
